Senses.PreferredTarget: Complete as vast space, lacking nothing and with nothing extra.
AlternateTargets: Round as the great void, neither deficient nor excessive.
SearchAliases: complete like vast space nothing lacking
great void neither deficit nor excess
Senses.Note: The Xinxin Ming compares the matter to vast space, lacking nothing and having nothing extra. Wuyi applies it to an openness that does not hold a fixed position. Baoning and Xuzhou question whether repeating the balanced words creates another division. Tanfang sets their completeness beside summer heat and flying ice; Weilin asks how it works when a teacher leaves one monastery and reaches another. Xuansha says the patriarch has stated only half. The phrase invites an immediate test rather than a claim that every situation feels equally comfortable.

Senses.Explanation: The paired clauses compare completeness to vast space and rule out both deficit and surplus. Wuyi applies the old line to openness; Baoning and Xuzhou press on the danger of stopping with its balanced wording. Senses.Note: The scriptural line says that complete bright knowing does not depend on a thought about it. A monk asks Ruibai how such knowing can be understood, and Ruibai answers with movement that follows an old road rather than a theory. Another monk offers the phrase to Shiyu, who replies with thirty blows. Wuyi voices it after speaking of eating together, drinking when thirsty, and sharing warmth and sleep. Pinjixiang raises a bamboo strip, quotes the line, and asks what further response is possible. These uses test the hearer's present knowing rather than the ability to repeat a claim about thought.

Ruibai and Shiyu answer monks who bring the line to them; their responses refuse an easy conceptual answer. Wuyi voices the line after eating, drinking, warmth, and sleep; Pinjixiang makes it a question with a bamboo strip.

Jiantang's shocking shop image rejects a comforting remedy and presses the listener to meet an unsettling Chan response directly. One original Tier-3 lamp witness and three active Tier-2 comments. Poshan, Huijueyi, and Pufuzhuo quote the verse and each challenge merely selling or imitating its dead-cat remedy. Linwo attributes similar words to Yuantong Ne; his witness is excluded pending source identity resolution. The dead cat head is an image in a Chan challenge, not a literal prescription.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Complete accord has no two shores; the nature of things has nowhere to return
SearchAliases: complete accord has no two shores; the nature of things has nowhere to return
Senses.Note: A monk asks Changsha how to turn mountains and rivers toward himself; Changsha asks how to turn himself into them. His verse says that complete accord has no two shores and the nature of things has nowhere to return. Tian'an adds a verse questioning both turns; Tui'an answers either direction the same way. Ying'an says Changsha failed to test the monk fully, while Shuzhong finds the exchange murky but revealing. The couplet challenges the assumption that one side must travel to the other.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB300.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong. Chaozong Tongren speaks at the close of a hundred-day retreat, on the birthday of the Great Compassionate One, in an address requested by layman Zhang Taofang to celebrate his father's longevity. Birds call everywhere in the second month; the gate of all-pervading hearing stands open, so why maintain a separation as great as clouds from mud? Yushan Shangsi raises Yunyan asking Daowu what the Great Compassionate One does with so many hands and eyes. Daowu compares their use to reaching behind one's back for a pillow at night, but corrects Yunyan's description from hands and eyes throughout the body to the whole body being hands and eyes. Yushan criticizes both formulations as sleepy talk, proposes responding to suffering and seeking its sound, and asks where Guanyin is now. After a shout he gives the headword: the gate stands wide open, so why the gulf between clouds and mud? The present cap challenges a separation maintained even amid responsive hearing; it is Yushan's own utterance, not part of either older master's answer.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin recalls asking Wuzu about the Second Patriarch's inability to find the mind and being told to investigate for himself. He recounts a later breakthrough, after which familiar cases and even bells, drums, donkeys and dogs disclosed the same message. Only then, he says, did he understand Tianyi Yihuai's verse: night birds call, the gate of all-pervading hearing stands open, so why remain separated like clouds and mud? The exact couplet belongs to the explicitly named earlier Tianyi; Yuanwu actively applies it to his own account of recognition. His surrounding warnings about contrived gestures and lingering judgments prevent the verse from certifying every sensory experience as sufficient.

Senses.Note: Other predicates retain the same rounded form while attaching different claims to it. Qianyan Yuanzhang pairs “perfectly round” with “shining and flashing,” then says “large within large, narrow within narrow.” Hongzhi Zhengjue says that the form is neither the least bit deficient nor the least bit excessive. Chunan Furong Baining Yi also criticizes a fixed reading: he says later people take “the perfectly round and shining one” as the ultimate rule, yet do not know that the Way has no fixed body and that heading toward it goes astray. His warning prevents the dictionary from converting a recurrent description into one universal abstract definition. The adverbial form occurs 15 times in 11 texts, and the exact round-and-shining pairing occurs three times in three texts.

Senses.Explanation: Something described this way is perfectly round on every side, with no edge, corner, or seam. The expression is attested. Hongzhi Zhengjue supplies the clearest physical constraint by saying that it is perfectly round and has no edges or corners. Shuzhong Wuyun applies the description to a begging bowl, calling it round and shining before describing where he throws or stores it. Yinyuan Longqi makes the same shape mobile by comparing it to a pearl running on a tray and a tray moving under the pearl; he then calls it perfectly round and lively, emerging and disappearing and opening and folding. In a separate three-part exchange, Yinyuan answers “what is buddha?” with “perfectly round,” “what is the teaching?” with “lively and active,” and “what is the monastic community?” with “freely at ease.” Zen bends a visible round, cornerless form into public answers and paired descriptive formulas, but the headword itself does not name one hidden substance, attainment, or universal abstract meaning.

Senses.Note: Flour is visibly distinct from snow despite the shared whiteness; coal is far harder to pick out from ink because both are black. Masters use this contrast after asking whether two responses, two teachers, or two ways of seeing are really the same. Fushi and Sixin place it directly at the point of a same-or-different question. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 尊便下座。師豎起拂子云：世尊三昧．文殊三昧總在拂子頭上，諸人還見麼？臥龍纔奮迅，丹鳳便翱翔。上堂，舉僧問巴陵：祖意教意，是同是別？巴陵云：雞寒上樹，鴨寒下水。白雲師，祖云：巴陵只道得一半，白雲則不然，掬水月在手，弄花香滿衣。師拈云：白雲盡力道，只道得八成。有問靈隱，只向它道：人我無明一丳穿。上堂：天不言四時行，地不言萬物生，拄杖子不言佛祖榜樣。是汝諸人長期百二十日，還曾夢見也未？禹力不到處，河聲流向西。密庵先師忌日拈香。百丈耳聾，黃檗吐舌，後代兒孫，半生半滅。破沙盆，曾漏泄，炎天六月飄霜雪。上堂，舉雪峰拈拄杖示眾云：我這箇只為中下機人。時有僧出問：忽遇上上人來時如何？雪峰擲下拄杖。後雲門云：我不似雪峰打葛藤。驀拈拄杖云：我這箇只為中下機人。有僧問：忽遇上上人來時如何？門便棒。師云：大機圓應，大用直截。雪峰．雲門只得一橛。畢竟如何？不說，不說。上堂。仰面不見天，低頭不見地，眉毛在眼上，鼻孔裏出氣，於我衲僧門下正好喫痛棒。為甚如此？易分雪裏粉，難辨墨中煤。喝一喝。上堂，舉：睦州見僧來參，便喝云：上座如何偷常住菓子？僧云：某甲方來，因甚道偷常住菓子？州云：贓物現在聻？師頌云：傾盡寶山寶，全身入荒艸。若是鳳凰兒，不向那邊討。上堂。萬法是心光，諸緣惟性曉，本無迷悟人，只要今日了。拍禪床一下，云：今日了，大盡三十日，小盡二十九。上堂：靈隱開爐，火種全無。將無作有，孰辨精粗？擬議烏藤劈脊摟，從教箇箇觜盧都。出鄉歸，上堂：東過西，西過東，主中賓，賓中主。大地全收，千差一舉。打鼓普請看，通身是泥土。上堂。千人排門，不若一人踏關；一人踏關，千人萬人皆到無疑安樂之地。與麼告報，莫有不甘者麼？良久，云：入水見長人。上堂：葉落歸根，來時無口。神仙玅訣，父子不傳。且如何道得接手句？多處添些子，少處減些子。上堂。今朝十五，陞堂直舉。全主全賓，燈籠露柱。不是佛，不是祖。剔起兩莖眉，三更日卓午。浴佛，上堂。年年此日潑惡水，箇事從悉達多起，自云徧界獨稱尊，後代兒孫誰管儞？上堂，舉：教中道：若謂如來有所說法，則為謗佛。且如黃面老子七處九會，當為何事水長船高？上堂，舉雲門大師道：釋迦老子與天帝釋在中庭相爭，佛法正閙。師云：雲門大師大似巧媳婦，等閑做出無󳫹䬪飥。雖然如是，人人也少一分不得。上堂：忽雨忽晴，天平地

Senses.Explanation: It is easy to open the mouth about how a matter begins and ends; it is hard to keep a steady heart when winter comes. The season stands for a test over time. Guxue gives the pair after a monk offers polished language. Muyun replies with it when a monk still does not understand a prior blow. Linye uses it against another stock formulation. Xueguan gives it in a written answer on wealth and practice. In each, the line tests whether words will endure as conduct.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB306.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Neishaozhong. At the Lantern Festival, Neishao Zhizhong moves from one lamp illuminating many lamps and one moon appearing in many waters to the denial that the many are truly more or the one less. The moon does not descend and the waters do not rise. He then gives the towers' fires and the traffic of people watching people. The public scene concretely carries the relation of one and many, while his questions about light before its flame appears keep the image from becoming a simple count of lanterns.

Lan'an Dingxu raises the Buddha's flower and Kashyapa's smile beside Mazu taking the seat and Baizhang rolling the mat, comments on their riches and effort, and warns that without a listener who knows the tune, such talk is futile. Asking how the ancestral intent is to be displayed on the fifteenth day, he answers with the fire-and-traffic pair. The festival's visible life answers the demand without a further explanatory theory of the ancient gestures. It does not mean every passing spectator has thereby understood them.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1376.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chijue Daochong. A monk quotes the festival pair to Chijue Daochong and asks how not to be carried about by appearances. Chijue repeats it as his answer. Later, in the address, he explains that fire illuminating fire leaves no darkness to find, and people seeing people leave no self-mark to find. He nevertheless asks why one house lights its lamps while another sits dark and urges seeking within oneself rather than elsewhere. The exact repeated scene is the teacher's active reply, and its later qualification prevents reducing it to either mere spectacle or a denial that different people have different responses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. Wuzhun Shifan opens with the same pair but sets fire aside to examine the people: they can look at other people, he says, but cannot look at themselves. If they could, they would have nowhere to put their faces. He ends with a reference to Touzi's words rather than explaining a special mirror for self-inspection. The festive traffic is redirected toward the hearers' own position, not offered simply as a picturesque celebration or a judgment that watching others is always wrong.

At the Lantern Festival, Neishao Zhizhong moves from one lamp illuminating many lamps and one moon appearing in many waters to the denial that the many are truly more or the one less. The moon does not descend and the waters do not rise. He then gives the towers' fires and the traffic of people watching people. The public scene concretely carries the relation of one and many, while his questions about light before its flame appears keep the image from becoming a simple count of lanterns.

A monk quotes the festival pair to Chijue Daochong and asks how not to be carried about by appearances. Chijue repeats it as his answer. Later, in the address, he explains that fire illuminating fire leaves no darkness to find, and people seeing people leave no self-mark to find. He nevertheless asks why one house lights its lamps while another sits dark and urges seeking within oneself rather than elsewhere. Senses.Explanation: At the Lantern Festival, Neishao Zhizhong moves from one lamp illuminating many lamps and one moon appearing in many waters to the denial that the many are truly more or the one less. The moon does not descend and the waters do not rise. He then gives the towers' fires and the traffic of people watching people. Senses.Explanation: The phrase denotes awakening characterized as sudden rather than staged gradually. Huineng says one's own nature awakens itself, with sudden awakening and sudden refinement and no gradual sequence. An unnamed monk contrasts sudden awakening of principle with gradual removal of affairs and asks Sanzu Chonghui for its principle. A case narrative describes Bao'en Xuance awakening suddenly at the fire-boy answer. Guxue Zhe likewise contrasts principle, which must be awakened to suddenly, with affairs removed gradually. Yongming Yanshou places sudden awakening in a fourfold matrix with gradual awakening and sudden or gradual refinement. Guifeng Zongmi defines turning from ordinary person to sage as sudden awakening. Yulin Tongxiu asks whether an addressee has the capacity for sudden awakening and sudden refinement. These uses distinguish sudden awakening from later refinement without forcing every record into one historical classification.

Senses.Explanation: A paired contrast, literally 'sudden and gradual.' The term is attested. The Platform Record reports that people spoke of Southern Huineng and Northern Shenxiu and therefore made a Southern/Northern division of sudden and gradual. Huineng's recorded correction is explicit: 'The teaching is originally one lineage; people are northern and southern. The teaching is one kind; seeing has slowness and speed. What is called sudden and gradual? The teaching has no sudden and gradual; people are sharp and dull, and therefore it is called sudden and gradual' (法本一宗，人有南北。法即一種，見有遲疾。何名頓漸？法無頓漸，人有利鈍，故名頓漸). Another recension puts it as 'seeing slowly is gradual, seeing quickly is sudden' (‘seeing slowly is gradual; seeing quickly is sudden’), again followed by 'the teaching has no gradual and sudden'. Later texts likewise say that sudden and gradual have no difference (頓漸無殊), or that whichever order is stated—'gradually refining, suddenly understanding' (漸修頓悟) or 'suddenly understanding, gradually refining' (頓悟漸修)—one must finally arrive personally once. The Record of the Source-Mirror enumerates four textual combinations: gradually refining and suddenly understanding, suddenly understanding and gradually refining, gradually refining and gradually understanding, and suddenly understanding and suddenly refining. That list records combinations of words; it does not override the Platform Record's direct correction or establish a hierarchy. The corpus contains five occurrences of 'the teaching has no sudden and gradual' (法無頓漸).
